newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Deal boosts interest in Burns Philp.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deal boosts interest in Burns Philp.

text.p: Settlement of the long-running Estate Mortgage dispute would free up Burns Philp & Co Ltd to concentrate on its core business but had also raised speculation about a takeover bid, analysts said on Thursday.

News of the deal lifted the Australian yeast and spice group's share price 10 cents to A$2.54, four cents above the price paid last month by New Zealand investor Graeme Hart to build up a 19.9 percent interest.

The A$115 million settlement was in line with expectations and would allow management to concentrate on the sale of the herbs and spices units and improving operations in the remaining businesses, analysts told Reuters.
"It does open them up for a takeover from the point of view that Hart has taken a large stake in the company," added a Sydney-based analyst, who declined to be identified.
"There's that sort of speculation flying around," he said.
The legal dispute followed the A$600 million collapse of the Estate Mortgage Trusts in 1990, wiping out the retirement savings of about 56,000 elderly investors.

The new trustees of the renamed Meridian Investment Trust sued the former trustee company Burns Philp Trustee Co, its parent, Burns Philp, former directors, insurers and advisers in an effort to recover the funds.
Burns Philp said it had agreed to settle all claims by paying Meridian A$90 million in cash out of existing reserves and issuing 12 million convertible notes at A$2.20 each.
Meridian, which is managed by Tyndall Australia Ltd -- 52 percent owned by Sir Ron Brierley's Guinness Peat Group -- said the settlement was worth a minimum A$116.4 million.
Burns Philp chairman Alan McGregor said he was pleased all claims against the company had been settled as it would allow the group to concentrate fully on its businesses.
"Estate Mortgage has taken up many hours of management time and the costs associated with mounting a complex legal case such as this are significant," McGregor said.
Legal sources said the court case, which began in February, is estimated to have cost in total up to A$24 million.
Burns Philp currently has its North American and European herb and spice businesses on the market after an unsuccessful attempt to become a global player.
The company is also looking for a new chief executive to replace Ian Clack, who announced he would step down in May.
Analysts said Hart was expected to take an active role in Burns Philp following the settlement, possibly seeking a suitor among overseas yeast or bakery companies.
Hart paid A$2.50 a share for his stake in Burns Philp in June when it was trading slightly above A$2.00. Monday's deal marked the first time it has since closed above A$2.50.
The company had a market capitalisation of A$1.347 billion based on its A$2.54 closing price, with 530.43 million shares on issue.
Burns Philp, meanwhile, sought a week's adjournment of the legal case on Monday and legal sources said it was likely Meridian would attempt to reach an out-of-court settlement with other parties.
Meridian settled with Estate Mortgage's auditors Priestley & Morris in April, receiving a A$31 million payout.
Units in the listed Meridian Investment Trust, which united and rationalised the old Estate Mortgage loan portfolio, closed eight cents firmer at A$1.55.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
